0.title: The Architecture of Redemption
0.essay:
Covenant theology is not an option for the academically inclined. It is the framework within which the whole Bible makes sense, binding Genesis to Revelation into one story.

One drama

Without it, Scripture can become a collection of disconnected stories, inspiring perhaps, but without the inner logic that holds it together. With it, every part of the Bible finds its place in one God-directed drama, whose theme is the triune God binding himself, by oath and blood, to a people he has chosen, redeemed and is bringing home.

What a covenant is

A covenant in the biblical world was not merely a contract between equals. It was a solemn, oath-bound relationship, often sealed with a sacrifice, that created a bond of loyalty, obligation and belonging. When the infinite, self-sufficient God enters into covenant with his creatures, binding himself by his own oath, on his own initiative and at his own cost, it is staggering condescension. “I will be your God, and you shall be my people” is the covenant formula, and it echoes from Eden to the new Jerusalem.

The Westminster Confession puts it beautifully: “The distance between God and the creature is so great, that although reasonable creatures do owe obedience unto him as their Creator, yet they could never have any fruition of him as their blessedness and reward, but by some voluntary condescension on God’s part, which he hath been pleased to express by way of covenant.”

Two Testaments, one story

Covenant theology is the Reformed answer to the question of how the Old Testament relates to the New: as promise to fulfilment, shadow to substance, type to reality, within one overarching covenant of grace administered differently across the ages. That is why the Old Testament can be read as Christian Scripture. Its covenants, ceremonies and prophecies all point to Christ: “For all the promises of God find their Yes in him” (2 Corinthians 1:20).

The tradition

The Reformation recovered justification by faith. The Reformed theologians who followed developed covenant theology as the biblical framework within which justification makes sense. Johannes Cocceius, Herman Witsius and Francis Turretin showed that Scripture is not a random sequence of eras but a single, progressive, covenant-shaped drama, and the Westminster Assembly built this into its Confession and Catechisms. This study draws on Witsius, John Murray, O. Palmer Robertson, Michael Horton, Geerhardus Vos, Calvin and Owen, and more recent voices such as Sinclair Ferguson.

Why it matters

Dispensationalism, which divides Scripture into distinct eras governed by different principles, remains common in popular evangelicalism. Covenant theology offers a more unified, Christ-centred reading, in which the people of God across all ages are one people, saved by one grace, through one faith in one Mediator. Understanding it transforms how you read your Bible, pray, and understand the church.

The chapters

The Covenant of Redemption, within the Trinity before time; The Covenant of Works with Adam; The Covenant of Grace, from Genesis 3:15 onwards; The Covenants in the Old Testament: Noah, Abraham, Moses and David; The New Covenant in Christ’s blood; and Covenant Theology and Baptism.

For reflection

Do you read the Bible more as a collection of separate stories, or as one story? What difference might it make to see it as the unfolding of God’s covenant?

1.title: The Covenant of Redemption
1.essay:
Before the world was made, before Adam drew breath, a covenant was made. Not between God and humanity, but within God himself: between the Father and the Son, in the Spirit.

An eternal agreement

In this eternal agreement, the Son undertook to enter the human story as the last Adam: to take human nature, to live the life of perfect obedience that humanity owed and could not give, and to bear the penalty for sins not his own. Reformed theologians call it the pactum salutis, the covenant of redemption. It is the ultimate ground of all salvation. The rescue of sinners was not an afterthought improvised in response to the fall. It was an eternal purpose, rooted in the love of the Trinity before time began.

The Father gives a people

This is not speculation. It is woven into Scripture. Jesus said, “All that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will never cast out. For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me. And this is the will of him who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day” (John 6:37–39).

The language of giving is covenantal. The Father has entrusted a particular people to the Son, and the Son has come to fulfil that commission. Here is the Father’s side (he gives a people) and the Son’s side (he receives them and pledges to lose none). In his great prayer, Jesus speaks again and again of “the people whom you gave me out of the world” (John 17:6), and of his authority “to give eternal life to all whom you have given him” (John 17:2).

The Son’s commission

Hebrews applies Psalm 40 to the coming of the Son. He says to the Father, “a body have you prepared for me” (Hebrews 10:5), and “Behold, I have come to do your will, O God, as it is written of me in the scroll of the book” (Hebrews 10:7). The scroll is not drafted at Bethlehem. The Son’s mission was determined in eternity; the incarnation is its enactment in time.

The context is the weakness of animal sacrifices, which could never take away sins and had to be endlessly repeated. The Son replaces them with a single, sufficient obedience and sacrifice. What was agreed in eternity is accomplished in history.

The Father’s promise to the Son

Psalm 2 is read throughout the New Testament as a conversation between the Father and the Son (Acts 4:25–27; 13:33; Hebrews 1:5). “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Psalm 2:7). And: “Ask of me, and I will make the nations your heritage, and the ends of the earth your possession” (Psalm 2:8).

The Father promises the Son a people from every nation, as the reward of his work. That promise underlies the Great Commission. The risen Christ says, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matthew 28:18), and sends his disciples to all nations. He is claiming his inheritance. Every convert from every nation is the Son receiving what the Father promised him before the world began.

The Spirit as the promised gift

The Spirit’s coming at Pentecost was not a surprise addition to the plan. Jesus said, “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper, to be with you forever” (John 14:16). And Peter explained Pentecost in exactly those terms: “Being therefore exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this that you yourselves are seeing and hearing” (Acts 2:33).

The Spirit is the Father’s promise to the Son, given at his exaltation, and poured out by the Son on his redeemed people. As Sinclair Ferguson shows in The Holy Spirit, the Spirit applies to God’s people what the Son accomplished for them.

The Son as surety

“This makes Jesus the guarantor of a better covenant” (Hebrews 7:22). A guarantor, or surety, takes full legal responsibility for another’s debt. The Son’s eternal agreement to stand as surety for his people is the foundation on which every other covenant is built. The Westminster Larger Catechism teaches that the covenant of grace “was made with Christ as the second Adam, and in him with all the elect as his seed.”

An objection

Some object that a covenant needs two distinct parties, so a covenant within the Trinity is impossible. But while Father, Son and Spirit share one divine being, they are genuinely distinct persons, and Scripture presents the Father and the Son in real covenantal dialogue (Psalm 2:7–9; Psalm 110:1; Isaiah 42:1–9; John 17). The language of giving and receiving, commission and obedience, promise and fulfilment describes a real eternal relationship.

Is my salvation secure?

The pastoral significance is immense. When a believer trusts Christ, they are not relying on a plan devised in haste, or on a decision they once made or a prayer they once prayed. They are relying on an eternal covenant, ratified in the blood of the Son who agreed before creation to be their Saviour. Their salvation is as old as God’s love, as certain as the Son’s faithfulness, and as invincible as the Father’s purpose. John Owen’s Communion with God beautifully explores how each person of the Trinity loves us in this work.

For reflection

How does it change your sense of security to know that your salvation was planned and promised within the Trinity before the world began?

2.title: The Covenant of Works
2.essay:
Adam stood in the garden not merely as a private individual, but as a representative of the whole human race. Understanding this unlocks both the fall and the gospel.

A probation in Eden

God placed Adam under a specific command, with life promised for obedience and death threatened for disobedience. “You may surely eat of every tree of the garden, but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat, for in the day that you eat of it you shall surely die” (Genesis 2:16–17). The principle was works: obey and live, disobey and die. Reformed theology calls this the covenant of works.

The text does not state the reward explicitly. But the tree of life in the midst of the garden (Genesis 2:9), and Adam’s later banishment from it (Genesis 3:22–24), show what was at stake: confirmed, everlasting life. And notice the generosity: every tree but one. The probation was not designed to be hard. It was the setting in which Adam’s loyalty could be expressed and confirmed. The tragedy is not only that he failed, but that he failed so easily, with so much given and so little asked.

Like Adam

Was it really a covenant? The word does not appear in Genesis 2. But Hosea says of Israel, “But like Adam they transgressed the covenant; there they dealt faithlessly with me” (Hosea 6:7). Some read “Adam” as a place name, but the force of the comparison is strongest if it refers to the first man: Israel was repeating the original covenant betrayal of its head. That implies Adam’s sin was itself a covenant violation.

Federal headship

This matters enormously. If Adam were only a private individual, his sin would be his own affair. But if he was a covenant head, a representative whose standing was the standing of all he represented, then when Adam fell, all fell. The Westminster Confession says that life was promised to Adam, “and in him to his posterity.”

That is exactly Paul’s argument. Death spread to all “because all sinned” (Romans 5:12), not merely in their own later sins, but in Adam, their head. And Paul draws the parallel that is his whole point: “Therefore, as one trespass led to condemnation for all men, so one act of righteousness leads to justification and life for all men” (Romans 5:18). “For as by the one man’s disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19).

Adam’s one trespass, counted to all he represented, mirrors Christ’s one act of righteousness, counted to all he represents. Deny the first, and you saw off the branch on which the second sits. John Murray’s work on Romans 5 shows this with great care.

The last Adam

“For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive” (1 Corinthians 15:22). Paul calls Christ “the last Adam” (1 Corinthians 15:45): a new covenant head, a new representative, a new humanity. And notice last. Christ is not merely a second attempt. He is the definitive, final head. There will be no third. His perfect obedience, atoning death and resurrection are permanently sufficient.

Every element of Reformed teaching on salvation hinges on this comparison: our sin counted to us in Adam, Christ’s righteousness counted to us in him; condemnation in Adam’s covenant-breaking, justification in Christ’s covenant-keeping. Christ did not only die for us. He lived the life of obedience that Adam failed to live, and that obedience is credited to all who trust him.

Was it gracious?

Some Reformed theologians hesitate to call the Eden arrangement a covenant of works, because God’s relationship with Adam was already one of kindness: creating and blessing him were gifts. The majority view keeps the distinction. God’s condescension in creating Adam was indeed grace. But the specific probation in Eden operated on the principle of works: obedience leading to life, disobedience to death. That does not make it graceless. It makes it different in principle from the covenant of grace that follows.

From works to grace

The Westminster Confession links the two directly: “Man, by his fall, having made himself incapable of life by that covenant, the Lord was pleased to make a second, commonly called the covenant of grace.” The covenant of works is the dark background against which the gospel shines most brightly.

The cost of denial

The doctrine is resisted today on several grounds. Some find legal representation morally objectionable. Others doubt that a covenant can be found in Genesis 2. But the cost of abandoning it is high. Without Adam as our representative, the parallel with Christ as our representative, the backbone of Romans 5, loses its logic. And to undermine that is ultimately to undermine the crediting of Christ’s righteousness to us, which lies at the heart of justification.

For reflection

Why is it good news, not bad, that we are represented by a covenant head? What does it mean for you that Christ obeyed in your place?

3.title: The Covenant of Grace
3.essay:
The covenant of works was broken the moment Adam ate. Justice demanded death. And yet the story did not end there. In the same scene, God spoke the first promise of the gospel.

The first gospel

To the serpent, God said, “I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring; he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel” (Genesis 3:15). This is often called the protoevangelium, the first gospel, and it is the beginning of the covenant of grace.

It was spoken to the serpent, not to Adam or Eve, because it is a declaration of war. At the end of the conflict stands one figure. He will strike the serpent’s head, a fatal blow, while the serpent strikes his heel, a painful but not final wound. The cross and the resurrection are here in seed form.

And the promise is entirely God’s. Adam and Eve contribute nothing. They stand in their shame and fig leaves while God speaks words that will take thousands of years to reach their fulfilment at Golgotha. Every later covenant unfolds this first promise, and the thread runs to the last pages of Revelation, where the serpent is finally defeated (Revelation 20:10).

What the covenant of grace is

The covenant of grace is God’s sovereign, gracious arrangement by which he promises to be the God of his people, to forgive their sins, to renew their hearts and to bring them to eternal life, not on the basis of their obedience, but by grace received through faith. Its mediator is Christ, the last Adam, whose obedience provides the righteousness the covenant requires.

Faith, the empty hand

The covenant of grace is not unconditional in the sense that nothing is required. Faith is required. But faith is not a meritorious work that earns the blessings. It is the empty hand that receives what God freely gives. And even that faith is God’s gift: “For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God” (Ephesians 2:8). The covenant of grace gives what it requires.

The gospel preached to Abraham

Paul makes an extraordinary claim: “And the Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham” (Galatians 3:8). The covenant with Abraham was not a preliminary, inferior version of the gospel, but the gospel itself. Abraham “believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6). The principle is the same as New Testament justification. “So then, those who are of faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith” (Galatians 3:9).

And the law, given 430 years later, “does not annul a covenant previously ratified by God” (Galatians 3:17). The heart of the Abrahamic covenant was never law, but faith receiving promise.

I will be your God

“And I will establish my covenant between me and you and your offspring after you throughout their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be God to you and to your offspring after you” (Genesis 17:7). That formula echoes through every covenant, and reaches its fulfilment in the last pages of the Bible: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God” (Revelation 21:3).

The covenant of grace has one content from beginning to end: God giving himself to a people as their God. Everything else — land, law, sacrifice, temple, kingdom — unfolds that central gift.

The new covenant promise

Jeremiah announced its fullest form: “For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the LORD: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they shall be my people” (Jeremiah 31:33). “For they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest, declares the LORD. For I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more” (Jeremiah 31:34). We will return to this in the chapter on the new covenant.

One covenant, many administrations

The Westminster Confession teaches that this covenant was “differently administered in the time of the law, and in the time of the gospel.” Under the law, it was administered by promises, prophecies, sacrifices, circumcision, the Passover lamb and other types. Under the gospel, by the preaching of the word and the sacraments of baptism and the Lord’s Supper. The difference is one of clarity and fullness, not of substance.

One people across the ages

This is what holds the two Testaments together. Abraham, David and the New Testament believer are all saved by the same grace, through the same Christ, foreshadowed or revealed, by the same faith. Paul can call Abraham “the father of all who believe” (Romans 4:11). Old Testament saints were not second-class members of a preliminary religion. They were saved by the same blood, applied to them in anticipation, and to us in retrospect.

Outward and inward

Under the old administrations, belonging to the covenant people outwardly was not the same as belonging inwardly. “For not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel” (Romans 9:6). Some were circumcised in body but not in heart. That distinction helps us understand the Bible’s covenant warnings and its accounts of apostasy. How it applies under the new covenant, where all its members are promised to “know the Lord,” is part of the baptism question we will meet in the final chapter.

For reflection

What does it mean to you that Abraham was saved by faith in the same way you are? How does Genesis 3:15 change how you read the rest of the Bible?

4.title: The Covenants in the Old Testament
4.essay:
The covenant of grace does not arrive fully formed. It unfolds through a series of covenants, each enriching the original promise without replacing it, each a new chapter in the same story.

A story with an ending

The covenant with Noah establishes a preserved creation in which redemption can be worked out. The covenant with Abraham names the people through whom the promised offspring will come, and the scope of the blessing: all nations. The covenant with Moses gives the redeemed people a law to live by and worship that points to Christ. The covenant with David narrows the promise to a royal line. Jesus said, “Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them” (Matthew 5:17). To read the Old Testament through its covenants is to read it as a story whose ending is Christ.

Noah: creation preserved

After the flood, God promised, “While the earth remains, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night, shall not cease” (Genesis 8:22). He made a covenant not only with Noah and his family but with every living creature, and gave a natural sign: “I have set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and the earth” (Genesis 9:13).

This covenant is unique. It is made with the whole creation. It is entirely unconditional. And its content is preservation, not salvation. God commits to sustaining the world so that his saving purposes can be worked out in it. It is the basis of what Reformed theology calls common grace: God’s good gifts to all people, which preserve human life and civilisation. Peter later uses the flood as a picture of final judgment (2 Peter 3:5–7), showing that the Noahic covenant points beyond itself.

Abraham: a people for all nations

God called one man out of paganism in Ur and promised, “And I will make of you a great nation, and I will bless you and make your name great, so that you will be a blessing” (Genesis 12:2). “And in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 12:3). From the very beginning, the particular served the universal.

The covenant is entirely one-sided. In Genesis 15, Abram cut animals in two, as was the custom for sealing a covenant. Then, “When the sun had gone down and it was dark, behold, a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch passed between these pieces” (Genesis 15:17). God alone passed between them, binding himself by oath to keep the promise, whatever Abram’s failures. God’s faithfulness, not Abraham’s, is the covenant’s foundation. Paul builds on this in Romans 4 and Galatians 3: the Abrahamic covenant is the charter of justification by faith and of the mission to the Gentiles.

Moses: law for the redeemed

The order of Exodus is decisive. The exodus comes before Sinai: redemption before law. God did not say, “Obey this and I will rescue you.” He rescued Israel, and then gave them his law as the pattern of life for a redeemed people. The Ten Commandments begin, “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery” (Exodus 20:2). God as Redeemer comes before God as lawgiver.

Sinclair Ferguson’s The Whole Christ shows why this order matters. Legalism begins when we tear the law from its setting in grace and treat it as a way of gaining favour rather than responding to favour already given. The Mosaic covenant is an administration of grace through law.

Yet it also had a sharper edge. Its blessings and curses in Deuteronomy 28–30 echoed the works principle, and Israel’s possession of the land depended on its obedience. Paul calls the law a “guardian until Christ came, in order that we might be justified by faith” (Galatians 3:24). It exposed sin, restrained it, and pointed forward to the one who would keep the law perfectly.

Reading the law

Covenant theology helps us read the Old Testament law. The ceremonial law — sacrifices, priesthood, temple — is fulfilled in Christ and no longer binding as ceremony, but still instructs us about him. The moral law, summarised in the Ten Commandments, remains the pattern of life for the redeemed, not as a way of salvation. And Israel’s civil laws expired with Israel as a nation, though they still teach principles of justice.

David: an eternal kingdom

David wanted to build God a house, a temple. Through Nathan, God turned it round: “the LORD will make you a house” (2 Samuel 7:11). A dynasty. God would raise up David’s offspring, “and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever” (2 Samuel 7:13). “And your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me. Your throne shall be established forever” (2 Samuel 7:16).

No merely human king could fulfil that. The prophets made clear that a coming son of David would reign for ever (Isaiah 9:6–7; Jeremiah 23:5–6; Ezekiel 34:23–24). David himself spoke of one who would be both his descendant and his Lord: “The LORD says to my Lord: ‘Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool’” (Psalm 110:1). The New Testament opens by calling Jesus “the son of David” (Matthew 1:1), and the angel told Mary, “the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1:32–33).

The prophets

The prophets could call Israel back to covenant faithfulness, pronounce covenant curses, and promise covenant renewal, because the covenants were the assumed setting of all their preaching. Without the covenants, the prophets become mere moralists. With them, they are heralds of a coming redemption.

For reflection

Which of these covenants helps you most to see Christ in the Old Testament? What does the image of God alone passing between the pieces tell you about his faithfulness to you?

5.title: The New Covenant
5.essay:
All the Old Testament covenants are arrows pointing forward, to a covenant unlike the old in its mode, yet the fulfilment of the old in its substance.

Announced in the darkest hour

Jeremiah announced the new covenant as Jerusalem was about to fall to Babylon and the temple to be destroyed. Into that darkness came a promise: “Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, not like the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt, my covenant that they broke” (Jeremiah 31:31–32).

“Not like” is important. The new covenant is not merely a renewal of the Mosaic covenant. It is new in the way it works. Hebrews explains: “For if that first covenant had been faultless, there would have been no occasion to look for a second” (Hebrews 8:7). The fault was not in the law, which “is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good” (Romans 7:12). The fault was in the people, whose hearts were hard. The new covenant deals with the heart.

New in three ways

First, it is written on the heart, not on stone. “I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33). The Spirit does from within what the law could only demand from without.

Second, all its members know the Lord. “And no longer shall each one teach his neighbor and each his brother… for they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest” (Jeremiah 31:34). The old covenant community was a nation joined by birth, mixing believers and unbelievers, where many needed to be told to know the Lord. The members of the new covenant are those who have been born again and know God personally.

Third, it rests on a complete forgiveness. “For I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more” (Jeremiah 31:34). Not the yearly covering of the Day of Atonement, but the once-for-all removal of sin by the sacrifice of the Son of God.

The new covenant in my blood

In the upper room, at the Passover meal, Jesus took the cup and said, “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood” (Luke 22:20). The covenant Jeremiah promised six centuries earlier was being inaugurated that night, by that man, through his death. Jesus identified himself as the Mediator of the new covenant, whose sacrifice would accomplish what all the old sacrifices could only point to.

The Passover, the covenant meal of the old, gave way to the Lord’s Supper, the covenant meal of the new. Each time the church gathers at the Table, it proclaims “the Lord’s death until he comes” (1 Corinthians 11:26), and believers are nourished by Christ, who is present by his Spirit to those who receive in faith.

A better covenant

“But as it is, Christ has obtained a ministry that is as much more excellent than the old as the covenant he mediates is better, since it is enacted on better promises” (Hebrews 8:6). Hebrews argues throughout from lesser to greater: a better priesthood, a better sacrifice, a better hope, a better country.

The old was good; the new is better. The old had priests who died and had to be replaced; the new has a High Priest who lives for ever to intercede. The old had sacrifices repeated daily and yearly; the new has one sacrifice: “For by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified” (Hebrews 10:14). The promise of a land becomes a new creation. A nation becomes a people from every nation. And “In speaking of a new covenant, he makes the first one obsolete” (Hebrews 8:13). To go back to the shadows would be a tragedy.

The Spirit poured out

At Pentecost, Peter explained that the Spirit poured out was the fulfilment of Joel’s prophecy. Then he called the crowd: “Repent and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. For the promise is for you and for your children and for all who are far off, everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself” (Acts 2:38–39).

The gift of the Spirit is the defining mark of the new covenant: not circumcision, not Torah observance, not ethnic descent, but the Spirit, received by those who repent and believe. The promise reaches as wide as the Abrahamic covenant — to them, their children, and those far off — and its scope is defined by the last phrase: “everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself.”

Continuity and discontinuity

Covenant theology holds both. Continuity: the same covenant of grace, the same Mediator, the same saving faith, the same people of God, the same moral law. Discontinuity: the ceremonial law fulfilled, Israel’s civil law expired, the covenant community now including Gentiles on equal terms, and a new covenant whose members all know the Lord. The newness is real, as Hebrews insists, but it is the newness of fulfilment, not replacement.

The early church

The first Christians understood themselves as the new covenant community from the start. The inclusion of Gentiles was not an afterthought but the fulfilment of the promise to Abraham (Galatians 3:14). The Jerusalem Council (Acts 15) concluded that the ceremonial requirements of the Mosaic covenant were not binding on Gentile believers.

What this means for us

The church is not a human organisation with spiritual ambitions. It is the new covenant community, the people of the last days, gathered into the covenant all the earlier covenants were preparing for. We are the most privileged covenant people in history: living on the far side of the cross and resurrection, in the age of the Spirit, reading Scriptures illuminated by their fulfilment.

For reflection

Which of the three “new” things about the new covenant means most to you? How might seeing the Lord’s Supper as a covenant meal change how you come to it?

6.title: Covenant Theology and Baptism
6.essay:
Of all the practical implications of covenant theology, none has caused more debate within the Reformed family than baptism. The question is whether the children of believers should receive the sign of the new covenant before they believe.

What is and is not disputed

Both sides agree that baptism matters, and that faith is necessary for salvation. Both agree that baptism is not a means of regeneration. Both agree that the children of believers are in a privileged position, and should be raised in the faith. The disagreement is about the nature of new covenant membership, and therefore about who should receive its sign.

The infant baptism case

The paedobaptist position, held by most of the historic Reformed tradition — the Westminster, Heidelberg and Belgic confessions — argues from the unity of the covenant of grace. It rests on three pillars.

First, there is one covenant of grace from Genesis 3:15 to the end. Second, under Abraham the children of believers were included and received the covenant sign: “He who is eight days old among you shall be circumcised. Every male throughout your generations” (Genesis 17:12). And the New Testament nowhere explicitly excludes them. Third, baptism parallels circumcision: “In him also you were circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, by putting off the body of the flesh, by the circumcision of Christ, having been buried with him in baptism” (Colossians 2:11–12). The sign has changed; the principle of household inclusion has not.

Paedobaptists add that circumcision always pointed to a reality not every recipient possessed: “But a Jew is one inwardly, and circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit” (Romans 2:29). So, they argue, baptism likewise places children within the covenant community as a pledge, with the prayer that the Spirit will make the sign a reality. They also point to the household baptisms in Acts, such as the Philippian jailer, who “was baptized at once, he and all his family” (Acts 16:33), and to Peter’s words, “the promise is for you and for your children” (Acts 2:39).

The believer’s baptism case

The credobaptist position, held by Reformed Baptists and expressed in the Second London Baptist Confession of 1689, argues from the newness of the new covenant. It also rests on three pillars.

First, the new covenant is a community of the regenerate. “For they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest” (Jeremiah 31:34), a promise Hebrews repeats for the church (Hebrews 8:11). Under Abraham, the covenant people were a nation joined by birth. Under the new covenant, its members are joined by new birth. The true children of Abraham are now defined by faith: “Know then that it is those of faith who are the sons of Abraham” (Galatians 3:7).

Second, every baptism the New Testament records follows a profession of faith. “Repent and be baptized every one of you” (Acts 2:38). Peter’s promise “for you and for your children” is defined by the rest of the sentence: “everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself” (Acts 2:39). And in the two household baptisms Luke describes most fully, the household is said to have heard and believed. Paul and Silas “spoke the word of the Lord to him and to all who were in his house” (Acts 16:32), and the jailer “rejoiced along with his entire household that he had believed in God” (Acts 16:34). “Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord, together with his entire household” (Acts 18:8).

Third, the sign should match the reality. Baptism signifies union with Christ: “Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life” (Romans 6:3–4). “For in Christ Jesus you are all sons of God, through faith. For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Galatians 3:26–27). These are realities only believers possess.

Credobaptists read Colossians 2 the same way. The “circumcision made without hands” is the Spirit’s inward work, and the passage goes on to say they were raised with him “through faith” (Colossians 2:12). So the true counterpart of Old Testament circumcision is not baptism as such, but the circumcision of the heart that God promised (Deuteronomy 30:6), and baptism follows the evidence of that inward work.

The verdict

Both positions are serious, biblical, and held by godly Reformed Christians. This study finds the credobaptist case more persuasive. The new covenant promises that all its members will know the Lord, and every baptism the New Testament records follows a profession of faith. The household texts are best read as households who heard and believed. So baptism is rightly given to those who make a credible profession of faith in Christ.

That conviction is held with charity towards brothers and sisters who differ. Believing parents of both convictions dedicate their children to God in prayer, raise them in the faith, teach them the Scriptures, and long for them to trust Christ for themselves.

History

Infant baptism was the consensus of the magisterial Reformers — Luther, Calvin, Zwingli and Bucer — and of the Reformed confessions. Believer’s baptism was held by the Anabaptists in the sixteenth century, and was developed with careful covenantal argument by the Particular Baptists of seventeenth-century England. Their Second London Confession of 1689 adapted the Westminster Confession closely, holding Reformed doctrine while arguing from the newness of the new covenant for believer’s baptism.

What both reject

What covenant theology rules out, on either side, is a thin view of baptism as merely a personal testimony to an individual decision, as if baptism were mainly about us rather than about God. Reformed paedobaptists and Reformed Baptists both understand baptism as an ordinance given by Christ, administered in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, which marks entry into the visible church and binds the baptised to Christ and his people. The disagreement is about who may receive it. The agreement is about what it means.

For reflection

What does your own baptism mean to you in the light of the new covenant? How can Christians who differ on baptism honour one another as members of the same covenant family?
